signalslink:block-handbooktext-blocksens:
The block sensor detects the presence of a block at a selected adjacent position and, based on its type or input signal, provides information about its state or slot occupancy at the output.
The currently supported blocks are:
Anvil - if there is a sufficiently hot ingot on the anvil for forging, the Output signal is 1. Otherwise, it sends signal 0.
Doors, gates, trapdoors - For doors and gates, you need to monitor the block at ground level on the hinge side. If the block is open, the Output signal is 1; if it is closed, the Output signal is 0.
A chest or any container in general, or any blocks that have inventory slots (e.g. a campfire, barrel, trough, etc.). The Output signal is determined by the input signal.
The input signal determines which slot is to be scanned.
Signals 1-14 specify slots 0-13. The output is information about the occupancy of the slot relative to the maximum stack capacity of the item in that slot, converted to a signal from 0-15.
Signal 15 specifies that the sensor should detect the total occupancy of all slots, e.g. the entire chest.
Any other block not listed above - If there is nothing in the monitored area (there is air), the Output signal is 0. If there is water, the output is 2-fresh water or 3-salt water. If there is any other block, the Output signal is 1.

Paper Conditions
Paper Conditions are relevant to the block sensor when monitoring containers or blocks with inventories in general. If you have set Paper Conditions, the behavior of the block sensor changes as follows: If you are monitoring a specific slot (input signal 1-14), the conditions are applied to the item in that slot and, if it matches the conditions, the signal set in the output instruction in the conditional block where the match was found is returned. If output is not specified, signal 15 is returned.
If you are monitoring the total inventory occupancy (input signal 15), the conditions are applied to all items in all monitored slots. As soon as an item matches the conditions, the signal set in the output instruction in the conditional block where the match was found is returned. If the output instruction is not specified in the conditions, the number of the first slot where a match was found is returned.
Tip: You can use this to find out the slot number. Place an item in the slot whose number you want to know. Leave the other slots empty, then monitor this block with a block sensor to which you apply the paper condition "*" and send signal 15 to its input. The output will then be the signal with the number of the slot containing the item.
If no item in the slots matches the Paper Conditions, signal 0 is returned.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-entitysen:
The Entity Sensor detects the presence of entities (players, livestock, wild animals, or monsters) in the marked area and can provide information on its outputs about their count, type, or status. The sensor requires charging with one or more Temporal Gears to operate. The consumption rate then depends on the size of the monitored area.
Inputs x, y, z determine the size of the monitored area in blocks.
On the Error output there is signal 1 if the sensor is discharged, otherwise 0.
Inputs Output 1 setting and Output 2 setting determine what information will be provided on outputs 1 and 2. You can thus obtain different information on each output, based on these input settings.
The options are:
1 - The output returns Count. The number of detected entities.
2 - The output returns Category. Bit flags of entity category 0–3: player, creature, animal, wild animal.
3 - The output returns Life state. All detected entities are: 1–dead, 2–alive, or 15–mixed.
4 - The output returns Sex. All detected entities are: 1–male, 2–female, or 15–mixed.
5 - The output returns Age. All detected entities are: 1–young, 2–adult, or 15–mixed.
6 - The output returns Species. All detected entities are: 1–player, 2–animal, 3–wild animal, 4–creature, or 15–mixed.
7 - The output returns Reproductive state. All detected entities are: 1–ready to mate, 2–pregnant, 3–lactating, or 15–mixed.
8 - The output returns Reproductive state flags. Bit flags 0–2: ready to mate, pregnant, lactating.
9 - The output returns Minimum generation. The minimum detected generation is: 0–15. Present entities without a generation specified are ignored.
10 - The output returns Maximum generation. The maximum detected generation is: 0–15. Present entities without a generation specified are ignored.
11 - The output returns Minimum weight. The minimum detected weight is: 1–starving, 2–low, 3–decent, 4–good. Present entities without a weight specified (not animals) are ignored.
12 - The output returns Maximum weight. The maximum detected weight is: 1–starving, 2–low, 3–decent, 4–good. Present entities without a weight specified (not animals) are ignored.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-managedch:
The Managed Chute enables automated item transport between different blocks. It transports items in only one direction, marked on the chute by a white arrow.
Unlike a chute, the Managed Chute has no inventory of its own and transports items from the block on the source side directly into the block on the target side. This means items are not stored in the chute, but merely transferred through it.
The Managed Chute has four Signals connectors: Input, Source, Target, and Output.
• Input controls transport. If the Input signal is 0, the chute is inactive and transports no items. A non-zero value at the input triggers transport of items from source to target. The following input values are supported:
1 - Transport one item
2 - Transport 2 items
3 - Transport 4 items
4 - Transport 8 items
5 - Transport 16 items
6 - Transport 32 items
7 - Transport 64 items
15 - Transport continuously.
Input values 1-7 allow items to be transported in batches. If the source block does not contain enough items to transport the requested amount, the chute transports as much as it can and moves the remainder only when another signal appears at the input. To transport another amount, different signal values from 1 to 7 can be sent to the input successively to compose the desired batch size.
Input value 15 causes the chute to continuously transport items from source to target, regardless of how many items need to be transported. The chute continues transporting items as soon as they appear in the source, until the input signal changes to another value.
Transport occurs when something is available for transport on the source side and there is room to store items on the target side. If either condition is not met, the chute attempts to transport items, but if this is not possible, it remains inactive until the situation changes (for example, items appear in the source or space is freed at the target).
• Source is relevant when the input block is a block with an inventory. In that case, the signal at Source determines which slot items are taken from. Signals 1-14 select slots 0-13. Signal 15 means items are taken from the last slot.
Signal 0 means items are taken from any slot. In this case, the chute searches all slots and takes items from the first non-empty slot. If the source block has no inventory, this input is ignored.
• Target is relevant when the output block is a block with an inventory or air. For an inventory, the signal at Target determines which slot items are placed into. Signals 1-15 select slots 0-14.
If the target block is air and there is ground beneath it, the following Target values are relevant: 1 - the chute attempts to place a block from the source onto the ground, 2 - the chute attempts to place an item on the ground if it can be placed. Signal 2 can also place a bucket including its contents; the bucket is not emptied.
The target ground directive on paper forces this attempt regardless of the Target signal. It first attempts to place a block or bucket, then possibly creates an item pile.
• Output reports what the chute sees at its ends. It is zero by default; its value is supplied by blocks with the output directive in Paper Conditions. Besides transport, the chute therefore also acts as a sensor and can control other machines.
Piles on the ground
The chute stores stackable items — such as firewood, ingots, boards, and others that can be piled on the ground — in piles. It creates a pile itself even on an empty spot and continues adding to it. A pile's capacity is determined by the item, not its stack size: one pile of ingots holds 64 pieces, even though ingots stack in chests in groups of 16.
When a pile is full, the target ground N directive allows it to continue one block higher, up to N blocks above the target position. The column stops at a solid block or when the new pile lacks support beneath it. Without a number, only the target block is filled.
Collecting from the ground works in reverse: the chute takes from the top of the column and removes emptied piles, so the column is dismantled from top to bottom.
Both operations can work in batches; see amount N below.

It can also collect layered blocks, such as fired charcoal. This is not an item pile, so the chute dismantles it layer by layer from the top. Conditions see such a column as an inventory, so its contents can be queried just like a chest.

If the source block is air, the chute collects floating items from a 3x3-block area whose middle block is the block in front of the chute opening. It can also pick up a bucket standing directly in front of the opening and insert it into the target inventory including its contents.

Building a firepit
The target firepit directive at the target position does not build a firepit from a finished block, but gradually as a player would: first dry grass, then sticks, and finally firewood. Each time, the chute takes only the material actually required by the next construction phase, so it does not stuff firewood into an unfinished firepit before there is anything to light it with.
A finished firepit is an ordinary target with an inventory, so fuel is added by normal transfer. It can then be lit by the Igniter.

Besides the above, the Managed Chute can also insert items of the type Ingot, Iron Bloom, and Blister Steel into an anvil if the anvil is placed on the chute's target side. When it inserts ingots onto an anvil, the plate forging recipe is selected automatically. For Iron Bloom and Blister Steel, slag forging is selected so that they become ingots. This is very useful for automating forging with an automatic hammer. Before inserting them onto the anvil, however, you must ensure that the inserted items are heated to the temperature required for forging. Conditions see the anvil as an inventory with one slot containing its workpiece. Therefore the in target scope works on it, including inventoryEmpty and inventoryFilled. The amount N directive inserts N pieces and is atomic: either all are inserted, or none are inserted and nothing is removed from the source.

Transport filtering
The Managed Chute allows conditions to be set for filtering items to be transported. Conditions are configured using Paper Conditions, whose use is explained on this page
signalslink:block-handbooktext-managedwa:
A Managed Chute embedded in a wall enables automated transport of items between various blocks. It allows transporting items through walls, which can be very useful for hidden transport systems or for moving items from a cellar or into a cellar without disturbing the cool cellar environment, important for long-term food storage.
It works on the same principle as the Managed Chute. You can therefore find the usage description on the page describing the Managed Chute.
signalslink:usageinfo-signalslink-text:
SignalsLink
Expands the Signals mod with additional components.

To monitor a block nearby, you can use a Block Sensor.
If you need to monitor your herd of livestock, the Entity Sensor is perfect for it.
If you want to automate some tasks, the Managed Chute will serve you well; it can transport items between blocks similarly to a chute, but you control it with signals and it gives you much greater control over what is transported. Its Managed Chute built into a wall variant allows items to be transported through walls, which can be very useful for hidden transport systems or for transporting items from or into a cellar without disrupting the cool cellar environment important for long-term food preservation.

Over longer distances and through ceilings or floors, items are transported by a Managed Damper, connected by a sleeve. You can extend the line with sleeve couplings. To pass through a wall, use a sleeve wall coupling. The damper can also place cargo on the ground and pick it up again, making it useful anywhere the chute cannot reach.

A Managed Valve is used to transport liquids. Connect it with a hose to another valve or to an intake in water; you can build longer lines using hose couplings.

An Igniter lights fires remotely. It fires a burst of sparks on signal and ignites whatever it is aimed at, so it can light a firepit without you having to stand there.

You control the behavior of all these devices with Conditions on Paper, which are shared by all of them.
signalslink:usageinfo-paperconditions-te:
Paper Conditions are a shared rule system for Managed Chutes, Managed Dampers, Managed Valves, and sensors. Write the rules on parchment and insert it into a supported device.
All these devices run on a shared core: the same syntax, the same evaluation process, and the same Output meaning. They differ only in what their source and target are and what they can do.

Basic principle
One paragraph on parchment forms one block. Separate blocks with one or more empty lines. Lines beginning with # or // are comments and are ignored.
All conditions in one block must be true simultaneously (AND). Blocks are processed from top to bottom.
Watch out for AND. Two conditions on the same code do not override each other; both must be true. This is useful: game:planks 5+ and game:planks 20- in one block mean between five and twenty. But it also means that a single impossible line kills the whole block. A classic case is game:planks * with a space: it looks like planks in any amount, but it is a pattern for a code containing a space, and no such code exists. The paper warns you about this; see Errors in paper below.

How paper is evaluated
One top-to-bottom pass does two things at once: determines the Output value and performs an action, namely a transfer or do seal.
Blocks are divided accordingly. A block with the output directive is an output block and transfers nothing; every other block is an action block. One pass can thus set Output and transfer something at the same time.
Three rules apply:
• The first valid output block wins; later ones are skipped.
• When no output block is valid, Output is 0. Output reflects the current state. Paper without a single output block therefore keeps Output permanently at zero.
• One action per pass is performed: the first action block whose action actually does work. A block that would transfer nothing (empty source, full target, invalid ifEmpty) falls through to the next block. This is what chains of blocks with target N ifEmpty, which fill slot after slot, rely on.
Order matters. Actions change the target state, so the same output block above an action and below an action responds differently in the same tick. It is up to you where to write it.
Likewise, block order overrides slot order: a block higher on the paper searches all slots it is allowed to, and only then lets a block below it act. Priority is determined by the paper, not by the chest layout.
A pass runs on every work tick of the device, even when it currently has no input signal, has nothing to transfer, or is waiting for its turn. This makes every device with an output block act as a sensor as well.

Devices and actions
• A Managed Chute transfers items between blocks at its two ends. It supports source, target, target ground, target firepit, amount, ifEmpty, do seal, and output.
• A Managed Damper transfers items through a sleeve and supports the same features as the chute. However, it has no Source and Target pins, so slot selection and ground mode are configured exclusively with directives.
• A Managed Valve transfers liquids from the remote end of a hose into its host. It supports source, target, amount, ifEmpty, do seal, and output. It does not transfer lava and cools hot water at the target.
• Sensors transfer nothing; their default action is signal output. Therefore every one of their blocks is an output block, even if you do not specify output; additionally, they understand output . for the number of the corresponding slot.

Code and attribute conditions
Exact code: game:resin. An asterisk * replaces any number of characters, and a question mark ? one character: game:log-placed-*, game:ingot-?. A regular expression begins with @, for example @^game:log-placed-(oak|maple)-.*$. The ! prefix negates the entire line, for example !game:resin or !game:firewood 96+.
A valid attribute name checks its truthfulness. Comparisons use >, >=, <, <=, =, ==: temperature>1100, stackSize>=16, durabilityRatio>=0.75. temperature, durability, durabilityMax, freshHoursLeft, and isSpoiling are also available.
The isBurning condition queries the block, not its contents: it is true when the given end is burning, such as a lit firepit or a smoldering firewood pile. It works in both scopes.
A bucket and other liquid containers provide isLiquidContainer, liquidContainerEmpty, liquidContainerFilled, liquidCode, and liquidLitres. For example, a full ten-litre bucket of water is selected by liquidContainerFilled, liquidCode=game:waterportion, and liquidLitres=10.
For liquids, patterns of both the world block and the liquid's internal portion work, for example game:water-*, game:water-still-7, *weaktannin*, or game:waterportion.

Inventory and amount
An inventoryAny condition checks any slot of the selected inventory, for example inventoryAny game:resin. It also checks liquids in liquid slots.
inventoryEmpty is true when the selected inventory is entirely empty. inventoryFilled is the opposite, meaning it contains something; it does not mean it is full to the brim. Both are especially useful with in target, where they check the state of the target rather than the transported item.
An amount pattern condition checks the total amount in an inventory: game:resin 10 means exactly 10, game:resin 10+ at least 10, and game:resin 10- at most 10. For liquids, the amount is in litres and can have at most two decimal places, for example game:water-* 50 or *weaktannin* 20+.
You can append slot N after an amount to query only one slot instead of the entire inventory: game:firewood 96+ slot 2. Slots are counted from one, just as with target N. A slot outside the inventory range is read as empty.
The difference is important: two slots with fifty firewood each total one hundred, so game:firewood 96+ is true, but game:firewood 96+ slot 1 is not.
A condition with a slot is a guard, not a selection. It queries the inventory, not the carried item, so it does not by itself qualify a block for transfer. This allows one block to transfer one thing while conditioning it on another.

Scope and transfer
in source switches conditions to the source inventory and is the default. in target switches them to the target inventory. You can alternate them in one block; a scope applies to the lines following it.
A block that is to transfer something must say what, meaning it must have at least one code condition in the source scope. If you do not care what it carries, write *. A block made only of in target conditions would have nothing to select by, and the paper reports this. This does not apply to a valve, where the source is the remote end of the hose.
source N selects the source slot and takes priority over the Source pin. target N selects the target slot, numbered from one. target N ifEmpty requires an empty target slot; after it is filled, the block falls through to the next one. target ground on a device aimed at air ignores the Target pin and attempts to place the item on solid ground; target ground N additionally allows the pile to grow up to N blocks above the target position. target firepit at the target position builds a firepit gradually according to what the next building stage requires.
amount N sets the size of one batch. For items, a batch is atomic: either the entire batch transfers, or nothing transfers and the block falls through to the next one. A batch can also be gathered from several slots with the same contents. A valve transfers up to the specified amount of liquid according to the source, target, and remaining buffer.
For ground piles, batches work in both directions. When placing, they can overflow into a higher pile in the column; when collecting, they are taken across several levels from the top, then distributed across as many slots in the target inventory as needed.

Output and sealing
output X sets Output to a value from 0 to 15. Output blocks always query the target, meaning the end where the device itself is located; you do not need to write the in target prefix in them, and in source makes no sense in them.
Resetting is automatic: when no output block is valid during a given pass, Output is 0. A resetting output 0 above filling blocks is therefore unnecessary. Older papers that have it continue to work; they just contain an extra block.
do seal seals the target barrel if it can be sealed. It usually belongs after filling blocks. A sealed barrel cannot be sealed again.

Errors in paper
Paper with an error is accepted, never rejected: one mistyped line must not stop an entire machine while you are still writing the rest. Invalid lines act as invalid, and errors are reported twice: immediately when attaching the parchment to a block and then permanently in the block's information window, in red above the conditions text.
The message always gives the line number and reason. It reports an unknown scope, invalid output, source, target, amount, or slot, an unknown action, an incomprehensible condition, and in source in an output block.
Two messages deserve mention because they reveal paper that looks correct but silently does nothing: a code pattern with a space and a block that does not say what it should transfer.

Examples
game:log-placed-*
target 3
Transfers wooden logs into slot 3.

game:water-*
target 2 ifEmpty
amount 50

in target
game:water-* 50+
do seal
First fills empty slot 2 with water. Once the slot is no longer empty, the first block falls through and the second seals the barrel.

game:water-*
amount 5
in target
inventoryAny game:log-placed-*
Pours water into a barrel in five-litre amounts, but only when it already contains a log — exactly for tannin.

game:ingot-copper
target ground 3
amount 32

in target
game:ingot-copper 192
output 15
Stacks copper ingots into a column three blocks high and reports 15 at Output once the column is full; one pile holds 64, so three hold 192. As soon as somebody starts taking from the pile, Output drops to zero by itself.

Setting conditions
Write conditions on parchment. Do not sign the parchment so you can edit the text again.
Transfer conditions into a supported block by right-clicking that block with this parchment. The conditions are stored in the block and can be seen in its information window when you look at it.
To remove conditions from a block, hold an empty parchment, crouch (Shift key), and click the block with this empty parchment. This deletes the conditions from the block.
If you want to copy conditions from a block onto empty parchment, right-click the block with empty parchment without crouching.
Finally, here is a tool to find out what code a block or item has and which attributes are available for use in condition expressions:
Hold the item you are interested in, hold the Ctrl key, and right-click a block that supports Paper Conditions with this item. The item's code and its attributes available for Paper Conditions are stored in that block. You can now copy them onto empty parchment as described above, freely edit them into condition blocks, and use them to configure the block.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-hosevalve:
The Managed Valve transports liquids through a hose. It always draws the liquid from the distant end of the line to its host. It has one hose anchor and two Signals connectors: the Input controls pumping, and the Output can be controlled using Paper Conditions.

Valve states
• Attached — the valve is placed next to a block with a liquid inventory, such as a barrel, bucket, or campfire. When there is a signal at the Input, it pumps liquid from the distant end of the hose into this host.
• Stand — the valve has no suitable inventory on its mounting side. In this state, it does not transport liquid; as soon as you place a suitable host block next to it, it attaches and starts functioning as an attached valve.
• Spout — a valve placed on the ground. When there is a signal at the Input, it releases liquid from the distant end of the hose; the liquid is not stored in the world, it is only displayed as droplets that soak into the ground. Useful if you need to get rid of excess liquid.

Pump control
Input signals 1 to 7 add a batch of 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, or 64 liters. Signal 15 pumps continuously. If two Managed Valves are active on one hose, they alternate pumping.
The valve does not transport lava and cools hot water at the destination to the ambient temperature. Paper Conditions can filter the transfer, change the batch size, seal the destination barrel, or set the Output to a value from 0 to 15.
signalslink:ingameerror-hose-anchor-occu: This anchor already has a hose.
signalslink:ingameerror-hose-same-block: A hose can't connect two anchors of the same block.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-hoseintak: The intake is a passive source of water or salt water. Place it in water and connect it with a hose to a Managed valve, which will pump the liquid from it. Longer lines can be extended using hose couplings.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-hosecoupl: A hose coupling connects two sections of hose and extends the line between Managed valves or intakes. One section of hose can be at most 10 blocks long.
signalslink:item-handbooktext-hose: A hose connects the hose anchors of Managed valves, hose couplings, and intakes. One section can be at most 10 blocks long; couplings allow the line to be extended over a greater distance.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-igniter:
The Igniter lights fires in the adjacent block. When triggered by a signal, it fires a burst of glowing sparks in the direction it is aimed and ignites whatever they land on — a firepit, a pile of logs, or another flammable spot. If the adjacent block is air, the sparks fall downward until they hit a flammable spot or go out after three meters.
It requires charging with temporal gears (Temporal gears) to operate. Insert a gear by clicking it; you can see how many bursts remain in the information window. Every shot costs the same, whether it ignites something or misses.

Connectors
• The input triggers a shot. It responds to the rising edge, meaning a transition from zero to a non-zero value: each signal means exactly one burst of sparks. The igniter deliberately has no continuous mode, so a signal forgotten at fifteen does not burn through the entire supply of gears.
• The output reports the result of the last shot: 1 when ignition succeeded, 0 when it did not or when there was nothing to fire. This can be used to repeat the attempt or send the machine onward.

Aiming
The Igniter can be placed freely, similarly to the Block Sensor, and clicking it switches the aiming direction:
• straight — sparks fly directly in front of the barrel;
• diagonally — sparks fly to the side at an angle, which is useful when something cannot be placed in front of the igniter.
Sparks follow an arc and fly for a while, so the igniter can also reach a spot somewhat lower down. Once the sparks land, the mod checks again what is actually at the landing spot — it may have changed before they get there.
signalslink:ingameerror-sleeve-anchor-oc: This anchor already has a sleeve.
signalslink:ingameerror-sleeve-same-bloc: A sleeve can't connect two anchors of the same block.
signalslink:ingameerror-sleeve-too-long: The sleeve can be at most {0} blocks long.
signalslink:ingameerror-sleeve-blocked: There is a block in the way of the sleeve.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-sleevedam: The Managed Damper transports items and blocks through a sleeve. It always draws the cargo from the distant end of the line to its host, so the active damper is the one receiving an Input signal. Mounted on a container it fills or empties it; standing on the floor it works with the block it faces, which lets it drop things onto the ground and pick them up again. It has only Input and Output pins - everything else, including slot choice and ground mode, is configured with Paper Conditions.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-sleevecou:
The sleeve coupling connects two sections of sleeve, extending the line between Managed Dampers. Each section may be at most 10 blocks long, and you may chain as many couplings together as you like.
The coupling itself controls and transports nothing; it only holds two anchors. Cargo flows through it without limitation, and it has no inventory of its own.
To route the line through a wall, wall in a completed coupling to create a wall sleeve coupling.
signalslink:item-handbooktext-sleeve:
A sleeve is a flexible conduit for items. It connects sleeve anchors on Managed Dampers and sleeve couplings, much like a hose connects valves.
To stretch a sleeve, take it in hand and click two anchors in sequence. A single segment may be no longer than 10 blocks; build longer conduits from couplings.
Unlike a hose, a sleeve must not pass through a block. The mod also monitors its path afterward: if someone builds a wall across it or soil collapses into it, the sleeve breaks and the conduit is interrupted. Keep this in mind for routes that run near a construction site.
To pass through a wall, use a sleeve wall coupling: attach a separate sleeve segment to each opening. The coupling connects the conduit inside the wall and lets you set the sealing of a cellar or room.
Cut a stretched sleeve with scissors.
signalslink:ingameerror-hose-too-long: The hose can be at most {0} blocks long.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-sleevewal:
The wall coupling lets you route a sleeve through a wall, floor, or ceiling. It connects just like a regular sleeve coupling.

Switch the seal by Ctrl + right-clicking with a pipe wrench in hand:
• cooling wall — for preserving cellar conditions (default setting);
• insulating wall — for retaining warmth in the room;
• open — without a seal.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-yardsign:
A sign on a post used to name a storage yard. Place it on any tile of the yard and write a name on it.
You do not need ink or a quill to write — the form opens immediately after placement, and you can change the name at any time by clicking it. The name may contain at most 24 characters so that it remains readable from afar.
The yard is named after the first sign standing on it. More signs on one yard are therefore fine, but only one of them determines the name.
The sign is also an ordinary marker — it controls nothing and has no connectors.
signalslink:block-handbooktext-yardtile:
A storage yard tile is ordinary paving on which goods are stacked. It controls nothing itself and has no state of its own; goods lie on it like ordinary stacks on the ground.
A continuous area of these tiles forms a storage yard — one unit that devices work with all at once, instead of having to point to each stack separately.

Shape and size
The shape may be arbitrary, as long as tiles connect along their sides — a rectangle, an L shape, around tracks, or around a building. Tiles touching only at a corner are not part of the yard.
A yard must have at least 4 tiles and at most 400. When the limit is exceeded, the yard is considered invalid and this is reported — nothing is cut off halfway.
Two yards that touch anywhere merge into one. If you want two separate ones, leave a gap between them.

How to tell what you built
Along the outer edge of the yard, a strip on the top side becomes lighter, making it clear how far the yard extends.
When you look at a tile, the information window shows how many tiles the yard has. That number is important — it immediately tells you whether two yards accidentally merged into one.

Naming
Place a storage yard sign on the yard and write a name on it. The yard can then be selected by name, which is useful when you have several of them next to each other at a station.

How much fits
Each tile holds one column containing one type of goods — a column is one slot to the paper, so types do not mix in it. If something else lies on a tile, the device skips it and tries the next one.
Only things that can be stacked into a pile belong on the yard. The device will not place anything that cannot be stacked there at all — it would lie on the tile as a placed block and could no longer be picked up.
How high a column grows depends on the cargo, not the yard: logs can be stacked high, while barrels should be in one layer so they remain accessible. Vintage Story also has its own limits based on item type, so some things cannot be stacked that high and the column fills sooner.

The Freight Dock is a crate that loads and unloads whatever is next to it. It is the first SignalsLink device with two endpoints of its own: one is itself, the other is the counterpart it finds beside it.
It has one undivided inventory with 48 slots. Each slot accepts both items and liquid, so you do not have to worry about what belongs where — Conditions on paper select by content, not by location.

The paper must say from where to where
Each block on the paper is under a header that names both endpoints:
• from X to Y — goods go directly from X to Y. The Freight Dock merely moves them; nothing needs to pass through the crate.
• unload X — shorthand for “from X into the crate”.
• load X — shorthand for “from the crate into X”.
An incomplete header is an error: from train without to is not treated as unload train, because guessing what you meant is the hardest kind of behavior to trace.
A header stands in its own paragraph and applies to all blocks below it, until the next header. The Freight Dock will not accept paper without a header and will tell you so — guessing what you meant would be the hardest error to trace.
After the direction, write which counterpart it is. Today that is yard, meaning a storage yard, followed by a cardinal direction and optionally a name from a sign:
unload yard
load yard north
load yard north northern pile
from train to yard north

How the counterpart is found
The yard is searched for within ten blocks of the Freight Dock. Without a direction and with a horizontal direction, it is searched for on two levels — at the Freight Dock's level and one block lower. The yard is flat, and the Freight Dock stands either on it or beside it on the same ground, so it cannot be elsewhere horizontally.
A cardinal direction (north, south, east, west) limits the search to that half of the surroundings. up and down search vertically, also within ten blocks: up for a Freight Dock buried beneath a platform with the yard above it, down for a Freight Dock above tracks or in the attic of a warehouse whose floor forms the yard. Without a direction, it searches all around.
When several yards are in range, the name on the sign decides; without a name, the nearest one is chosen. The search proceeds outward from the nearest surroundings, so a yard right next to it costs practically nothing.
The entire yard appears to the paper as one inventory, assembled from columns of stacks from the nearest tile to the farthest. It therefore fills from your end: the nearest column up to its height, then the next one.

How much is transferred
Without the amount directive, one operation transfers everything that matches. This is the reverse of other devices, and deliberately so: “unload the whole wagon” would otherwise take forever. The amount N directive applies unchanged, meaning exactly N items or nothing.
The amount N directive is atomic — N items are transferred, or nothing. If you want to transfer in batches but not stop when goods run low, write amount N- (at most N, and fewer are transferred too). If instead you want to wait for a full batch and then move everything at once, write amount N+ (at least N). The symbols mean the same as for conditions.
With the height N directive, you specify how high a column may be stacked. Height belongs to the cargo, not to the yard: logs can be stacked high, while you want barrels in a single layer so they remain accessible. It is a limit, not a guarantee — some things cannot be stacked that high and the column fills sooner.

Connectors
• Input provides credit. Signals 1 through 7 add 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, or 64 transfers; signal 15 operates continuously. One transfer costs one credit, whether it moves one item or a whole stack.
• Output reports what the Freight Dock sees at its endpoints; blocks with the output directive set its value. They are evaluated across the entire paper, and the first one that matches applies, regardless of which section it is written in.
Cancel unused credit by crouching and tapping with a pipe wrench.

Placement
The Freight Dock is placed rotated, like a crate or chest — it is placed with the working corner containing the connectors facing you. Without a signal at the Input, it only looks around and does nothing.
